part_title: AWS Security Recap, Bedrock Controls, KMS, SageMaker and Private Model Auditing

scenes.title: AWS Security Services: Section Summary
scenes.visual_overview: The slide combines identity, compute, network and storage in a conceptual architecture, then maps controls to four practical scenarios.
visual_walkthrough: Top arrow legend: requests/data, permission/control, service interactions
IAM users/roles are principals; IAM groups organize users
STS temporary role credentials to EC2/Lambda
VPC and private endpoint to Amazon S3
Bottom four choice panels for IAM, compute, networking and data
Security group, bucket policy, encryption/versioning notes
scenes.visual_example: Developers access authorized S3 and EC2 resources, applications run on EC2 or Lambda with roles, and private VPC endpoints can protect S3 access.
scenes.visual_synthesis: The diagram is an illustrative set of cooperating tools, not a mandatory service chain for every workload.
scenes.narration: This slide ties together the foundation services we have just studied and answers which control belongs at which architectural layer. Begin with the legend: blue arrows represent requests and data, purple arrows represent policy or permission control, and gold arrows illustrate interactions between services. On the left are IAM users and roles, which can act as request principals, and groups, which organize users and receive policies but are not principals themselves. Follow the arrow into IAM permission evaluation. Applications running on EC2 or Lambda can use roles and receive temporary session credentials via STS, avoiding embedded long-term keys. Move right into Amazon VPC and a VPC endpoint for private connectivity to services such as S3, which stores the actual objects. Now scan the four lower scenario cards. For user access choose IAM. For computation choose EC2 or Lambda according to the workload, and assign scoped roles. For private network paths consider a VPC and appropriate endpoints. For stored application logs or datasets in S3 use bucket policies, encryption and versioning as needed. The note above these cards is important: different applications use different combinations; this is not a compulsory pipeline. The overall picture separates authorization, computation, transport and stored-data protection.

scenes.title: Security Service Selection: Recap
scenes.visual_overview: Seven AWS security and governance tools are compared by the question each one answers, followed by an example flow.
visual_walkthrough: Seven top cards: Macie, Config, Inspector, CloudTrail, Artifact, Audit Manager, Trusted Advisor
Central AWS resource area with API requests, CloudTrail, Inspector and Config observation arrows
Compliance side to Artifact provider reports and Audit Manager evidence
Bottom customer-documents-in-S3 practical example
Exam cue choose service by sensitive data, state, vulnerability, activity, reports, evidence or best practices
scenes.visual_example: A company stores customer documents in S3, uses Macie for PII, Config for resource state, CloudTrail for API history, Inspector for compute vulnerabilities, Artifact for AWS provider reports, Audit Manager for its own evidence and Trusted Advisor for recommendations.
scenes.visual_synthesis: These tools complement each other; CloudTrail observes API events rather than acting as inline authorization.
scenes.narration: This slide is a seven-way service selection guide. Its main purpose is to stop similar-sounding AWS security tools from being confused. Read the seven colored cards across the top. Macie searches S3 for sensitive information. Config tracks supported resource configurations and rule evaluations. Inspector finds supported software vulnerabilities and EC2 network exposure. CloudTrail records API activity. Artifact provides AWS reports and agreements. Audit Manager organizes evidence about your workload against frameworks. Trusted Advisor recommends best-practice improvements. Now examine the lower middle flow. Users and applications issue API requests to AWS resources such as S3, EC2 and Lambda. CloudTrail records supported calls as an observer, not as an inline gate in the request path. Inspector examines eligible workloads, while Config tracks settings and history. The right side shows the different compliance branches: Artifact supplies provider reports, Audit Manager gathers your own evidence, and Trusted Advisor gives account recommendations. The bottom practical example applies every tool to one company handling customer documents, and the exam box asks you to match requirement to capability. The big-picture lesson is that data discovery, vulnerability management, API auditing, configuration compliance and assurance evidence solve different problems. No single one replaces all the others.

scenes.title: AWS Services for Bedrock
scenes.visual_overview: A customer-support application's Bedrock request is protected by IAM, configured Guardrails and separate CloudTrail/Config observation.
visual_walkthrough: Client application input arrow to Bedrock and response arrow back
IAM arrows authorize invocation and model-management actions
Guardrails input and output evaluations
CloudTrail API-activity logging and Config supported configuration changes
Colored legend for request, controls, guardrails and audit
Bottom support question password reset example
scenes.visual_example: A support application asks how to reset a password, IAM allows the Bedrock call, Guardrails evaluate input/output, CloudTrail records supported activity, and Config observes supported changes.
scenes.visual_synthesis: Authorization, content safeguards and audit records are separate; Guardrails do not guarantee perfect safety.
scenes.narration: This image shows four control families surrounding one Bedrock application rather than four steps that always run in a simple straight line. Start at the client on the left: a customer support app sends a question to Amazon Bedrock and expects a model response. The gold IAM arrows above govern whether the application's identity may invoke the selected model or manage related AWS resources. The purple arrows on the right show configured Bedrock Guardrails evaluating input and output content under their enabled policies. They can reduce unwanted content or disclosure but are not a guarantee that every unsafe behavior is blocked. The dashed audit arrows have a different meaning. CloudTrail records supported API activity for audit and security investigation, while AWS Config can track selected configuration state and changes where those resources are supported. Neither is the content-generation engine itself. Follow the practical example below: a user asks how to reset a password, the application invokes Bedrock with appropriate permission, guardrails evaluate relevant content and the app returns a help-center style answer. The audit signals are recorded separately. The legend distinguishes request flow, authorization, guardrails and observation. The overall picture shows defense in depth: permission to call, permitted content, traceable activity and managed configuration.

scenes.title: Accessing Encrypted S3 Data from Bedrock
scenes.visual_overview: A Bedrock model customization job needs a service role, S3 data permissions and KMS authorization to read SSE-KMS training data.
visual_walkthrough: User submits customization with S3 URI and service role
Bedrock service role calls S3 GetObject on training source
S3 uses KMS Decrypt and returns plaintext over TLS
Separate output bucket for metrics/logs
Bottom trainingDataConfig and outputDataConfig JSON
IAM S3 actions, KMS key policy and optional additional grants
scenes.visual_example: A Bedrock customization job reads s3://example-bucket/train.jsonl encrypted with an AWS KMS customer-managed key and writes training/validation metrics under s3://example-bucket/output/.
scenes.visual_synthesis: Both role and key permissions matter; SSE-KMS decryption happens on the service side, not by sending encrypted ciphertext to the model.
scenes.narration: This slide explains a specific permission problem: a Bedrock model customization job cannot read an SSE-KMS encrypted dataset in S3 unless the appropriate identities and encryption-key controls allow it. Start with the user on the left submitting a job that specifies a training-data S3 URI and an IAM service role. Follow the first arrow into Amazon Bedrock. The service assumes the authorized role and makes an S3 GetObject request using that role's permissions. The S3 bucket in the middle has server-side encryption with AWS KMS. Now trace the gold arrows to the KMS key: the authorized S3 operation needs decrypt permission under the relevant IAM and key policies. S3 performs the decryption server-side and sends the requested plaintext object over a protected TLS connection to the customization process. It does not require the model to decrypt S3 ciphertext itself. The separate lower arrow points to an S3 output location for training or validation results. The JSON snippet at the bottom shows trainingDataConfig.s3Uri and outputDataConfig.s3Uri as distinct locations. The permission panel calls out scoped s3:GetObject, relevant s3:PutObject and kms:Decrypt, with additional permissions or grants when required. The whole picture is an authorization chain across Bedrock, S3 and KMS, not just an S3 bucket ACL.

scenes.title: SageMaker VPC Connectivity and S3 Gateway Endpoint
scenes.visual_overview: Two different SageMaker private-network paths appear: caller-to-managed model hosting and model-container-to-private resources.
visual_walkthrough: Customer VPC 10.0.0.0/16 split into two private subnets
Upper SageMaker Runtime interface endpoint connects caller privately to AWS-hosted inference endpoint
Lower Model VpcConfig ENIs provide model container connectivity
S3 gateway endpoint via route table with S3 prefix list
Endpoint policy, IAM role and security groups restrict bucket/prefix
Right S3 training-data and model-artifact prefixes
Exam difference interface ENI versus gateway route target
scenes.visual_example: An application invokes a hosted SageMaker endpoint privately, while a configured model container accesses approved S3 model files through a gateway route where supported.
scenes.visual_synthesis: SageMaker hosting is managed outside the VPC; VpcConfig for private model resource access is distinct from a Runtime interface endpoint.
scenes.narration: This architectural slide makes a distinction that is easy to miss: SageMaker model hosting is an AWS-managed service, not merely an EC2 model server you placed directly in your private subnet. The diagram contains a customer VPC with two private subnets. Follow the upper purple route first. An application caller sends HTTPS to a SageMaker Runtime interface VPC endpoint in the customer's subnet. That endpoint provides a private path to the managed SageMaker model-hosting service shown on the right, outside the VPC boundary. Now follow the lower green route separately. A model configured with VpcConfig can have network interfaces in the customer's subnets so its container can reach authorized private resources. The S3 gateway endpoint is a different construct: the route table uses an S3 prefix-list destination and a gateway-endpoint target, rather than an interface endpoint network interface. The rightmost bucket lists training-data and model-artifact key prefixes. Review the three security boxes: the SageMaker role scopes data actions, the S3 gateway endpoint policy restricts service access, and security groups control relevant network paths. The bottom worked example and exam cue reinforce that caller-to-endpoint access, container VpcConfig traffic and S3 data access are related but distinct paths, each requiring correct configuration.

scenes.title: Private Application Access to a Bedrock Model
scenes.visual_overview: A private app uses private DNS and a Bedrock Runtime interface endpoint to invoke a model without internet or NAT.
visual_walkthrough: Private application and interface endpoint ENI in subnet 10.0.1.0/24
Step 1 HTTPS and private DNS to endpoint
Step 2 AWS private network to Bedrock Runtime and selected model
Endpoint security group, endpoint policy and IAM permissions
Bottom boto3 bedrock-runtime InvokeModel template
No public route/NAT needed for this API path
scenes.visual_example: An app in a private subnet calls the Bedrock Runtime API via its VPC endpoint; private DNS resolves the standard hostname to private endpoint IPs and the role permits InvokeModel.
scenes.visual_synthesis: PrivateLink changes the network path, not API body format or IAM authorization; model and Region must match.
scenes.narration: This slide walks through a private application calling Bedrock Runtime without sending the API request over the public internet. Start on the left inside the VPC address range 10.0.0.0/16. An app runs in private subnet 10.0.1.0/24 alongside a Bedrock Runtime interface endpoint, represented by an elastic network interface with a private IP. The first blue arrow is an HTTPS invocation. With private DNS configured, the standard Bedrock Runtime hostname resolves to the endpoint's private address. The second arrow carries traffic across the AWS network to the managed Bedrock Runtime API. The third arrow represents a call to the selected foundation model, which might be one of several providers supported in that Region. Now read the three permissions below the drawing. The endpoint security group permits HTTPS from the app, the endpoint policy can restrict actions and resources, and the app's IAM role must authorize required Bedrock Runtime operations. The boto3 example at the bottom is a template: the chosen model ID, content type and JSON request body must match the selected model's supported API. The final exam panel stresses that NAT or a public IP is unnecessary for this particular API path. Private networking and authorization both still matter.

scenes.title: Auditing Bedrock API Access with CloudTrail
scenes.visual_overview: CloudTrail records supported Bedrock API activity, with management and selected data-event categories plus optional longer retention.
visual_walkthrough: Principals IAM user, role or service invoke/list Bedrock APIs
Allowed and denied requests may produce recorded events
CloudTrail management event examples InvokeModel, Converse, Get/ListFoundationModels
Optional data event selection for InvokeAgent, RetrieveAndGenerate, ApplyGuardrail
Event history 90 days versus trail S3 delivery and data selectors
Bottom event JSON: eventSource, eventName, region, time, assumed role, sourceIP and errorCode
Caution CloudTrail not full prompt/response logging
scenes.visual_example: An assumed AppRole makes InvokeModel call; example audit JSON includes AccessDenied and sourceIPAddress, while no prompt contents are recorded.
scenes.visual_synthesis: Choose CloudTrail for API identity/time/action; enable Bedrock invocation logging separately when prompt or response records are required.
scenes.narration: This final slide explains how to investigate who used Amazon Bedrock and whether a request succeeded or failed. Begin with the principals on the left: IAM users, application roles and AWS services can make Bedrock API requests according to permissions. The central Bedrock panel lists example operations, including InvokeModel, Converse and model discovery. Green and red arrows both lead toward CloudTrail, showing that supported allowed and denied attempts can produce audit events when the relevant category is captured. Now read the two sections inside CloudTrail. Management events cover management-classified operations such as standard model invocation and listing; selected data-plane operations including InvokeAgent, RetrieveAndGenerate or ApplyGuardrail require explicitly configured data-event selectors. Exact classifications are operation-specific and should follow AWS documentation. The right panel contrasts recent Event history, which covers ninety days of management events in a Region, with a configured trail that delivers ongoing selected records to S3. Finally examine the worked JSON. It shows a Bedrock event source, InvokeModel event name, Region, time, an assumed application role and source IP, with AccessDenied as the example error code. This is audit metadata, not the user's full prompt or model response. For content capture, use separately configured Bedrock invocation logging with appropriate privacy controls. Together, this closes the module by separating permissions, private API transport and traceable usage.
